title: Weyl denominator identity in an integral character lattice
statement:
Let $X,Y$ be finite-rank free abelian groups (free $\mathbf Z$-modules in [def-weil-pbc-free-module]) with a perfect integer bilinear pairing $\langle-,-\rangle:X\times Y\to\mathbf Z$. Let $\Phi\subset X\setminus\{0\}$ and bijectively indexed $\Phi^\vee\subset Y\setminus\{0\}$ be a finite reduced crystallographic root datum: the roots and coroots span $X\otimes\mathbf Q$ and $Y\otimes\mathbf Q$; $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$; the reflections $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and the dual reflections preserve the respective sets and their bijection; and the only roots proportional to $\alpha$ are $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$. Fix a positive system $\Phi^+$ with simple-root base $\Delta$, meaning that every root has integer simple-root coordinates all nonnegative or all nonpositive, and $\Phi^+$ is the former set. Suppose $\rho=\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$ belongs to $X$. Let $W$ be the finite group generated by the reflections on $X$, and set $A(\nu)=\sum_{w\in W}\det(w)e^{w\nu}$ in $\mathbf Z[X]$, the free abelian group with basis $e^x$ and multiplication $e^xe^y=e^{x+y}$. The determinant is taken on $X\otimes\mathbf Q$. Then
$$A(-\rho)=e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^\alpha).$$
The empty root system and zero-rank lattices are allowed, with $W=\{1\}$ and product $1$.

proof.text: If $\Phi=\varnothing$, spanning forces $X\otimes\mathbf Q=0$. Freeness gives $X=0$, so $\rho=0$, $W=\{1\}$ and both sides are $1$. Otherwise identify $X$ with its image in $V=X\otimes\mathbf R$ using an integer basis. The roots span $V$ and the given simple-root base is a real basis: its rational coordinate matrix has the same rank over $\mathbf Q$ and $\mathbf R$. Reducedness persists over $\mathbf R$, since any proportionality scalar between two nonzero rational-coordinate vectors is rational. Choose a coordinate dot product $b_0$ and set $b(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}b_0(wx,wy)$. Reindexing makes $b$ invariant, and its identity summand makes it positive definite. From $b(s_\alpha x,s_\alpha\alpha)=b(x,\alpha)$ and $s_\alpha\alpha=-\alpha$ obtain $\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2b(x,\alpha)/b(\alpha,\alpha)$. Thus the real root set, this form and the given base meet the hypotheses of the cited real-root-system lemmas below. Determinants are unchanged by extension from $\mathbf Q$ to $\mathbf R$.

proof.text: For $\delta\in\Delta$ and $\beta\in\Phi^+\setminus\{\delta\}$, some simple coordinate of $\beta$ other than its $\delta$ coordinate is positive, since otherwise reducedness forces $\beta=\delta$. Reflection in $\delta$ leaves that coordinate unchanged. All coordinates of the resulting root have one sign, so $s_\delta\beta$ is positive and is not $\delta$ (its inverse image would be $-\delta$). Involutivity gives a permutation of $\Phi^+\setminus\{\delta\}$. Summing roots now gives $s_\delta\rho=\rho-\delta$ and hence $\langle\rho,\delta^\vee\rangle=1$. The form formula gives $b(\rho,\delta)>0$; by positive simple coordinates, $b(\rho,\alpha)>0$ for every positive root. In particular $\rho$ is regular and lies in the open chamber of $\Delta$.

proof.text: The coefficient $c_\rho$ is $1$: the empty subset contributes $1$; a nonempty subset of positive roots cannot sum to zero, since each root has positive total simple-coordinate sum. The orbit map $W\to W\rho$ is injective. Indeed any $w$ fixing the regular point $\rho$ maps its chamber to a chamber containing that point, hence to itself, and freeness in [lem-sfb-root-chamber-simple-transitivity] forces $w=1$. Applying this to $w_2^{-1}w_1$ proves injectivity. Step 3 gives $c_{w\rho}=\det(w)$, and step 5 excludes all other support. Comparing coefficients in the free abelian basis therefore proves $D=\sum_{w\in W}\det(w)e^{w\rho}=A(\rho)$.

proof.text: Apply the ring automorphism $e^x\mapsto e^{-x}$ (multiplicativity follows from $-(x+y)=-x-y$) to the last equality. It sends $A(\rho)$ to $A(-\rho)$ and $D$ to $e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^\alpha)$. This is exactly the claimed identity, including its sign.
